paper_title: AIRIS: Benchmarking Social Embodied Intelligence in Egocentric Streaming Videos

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Embodied agents operating around people must not only recognize social cues, but also decide when the available evidence is sufficient, whether to intervene, and how to respond without violating social norms. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate these abilities in isolation or with access to completed videos, obscuring where an online social decision fails. We introduce AIRIS, a causal streaming benchmark that formulates social embodied intelligence as a time-anchored chain of Attention, Intention, Reaction, and Interaction (A-I-R-I). AIRIS contains 8,000 expert-curated questions grounded in 357 egocentric clips across 11 context categories and 36 capability dimensions. At each query, models receive only the observation prefix available at that time; decision-aware metrics reward calibrated waiting and complete reactions while penalizing premature commitment. Evaluating 45 proprietary and open-source general-purpose, embodied, streaming-video, and omni-modal models reveals fragmented and temporally miscalibrated competence. General-purpose VLMs excel at passive cue grounding and intent recognition, whereas embodied specialists lead on isolated reaction sub-decisions; yet across all families, models frequently guess intents before sufficient evidence emerges and fail to jointly align intervention timing, action domain, and concrete execution within the same episode. AIRIS thus provides a diagnostic foundation for bridging the gap between passive social perception and reliable embodied interaction.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: An embodied agent sharing space with people must do more than recognize objects and execute commands. When person glances toward an object and begins gesture, the agent must determine whether the cue concerns it, infer what the person intends, and decide whether to act immediately, wait for more evidence, or refrain from acting. Even physically feasible response can be socially mistimed, intrusive, or incomplete. Such decisions arise continually in collaborative homes, public spaces, and assistive settings, where successful behavior depends on both task competence and sensitivity to people [13]. We conceptualize the ability to perceive, interpret, and act appropriately within these evolving interpersonal situations as social embodied intelligence [46]. To date, the community has successfully operationalized distinct facets of this intelligence through specialized, domain-specific tasks, as shown in Table 1. For instance, research in streaming and proactive video evaluates models under continuous input, emphasizing strict observation prefixes and timely intervention [710]. Meanwhile, multimodal social benchmarks dive deep into interpreting gaze, gesture, intent, and latent mental states in natural human interactions [1114]. In parallel, norm-aware embodied evaluations assess whether proposed actions are permissible and compatible with hidden constraints during ongoing human activities [1518]. However, existing evaluations often assess social cues, intent, response appropriateness, and interaction outcomes separately. This separation makes it difficult to characterize these capabilities within the same unfolding interaction. unified evaluation with shared episodes and temporal anchors would enable systematic comparison of stage-specific strengths and weaknesses. To address this mismatch, we introduce AIRIS, streaming benchmark that evaluates social embodied 1 Figure 1 AIRIS: evaluating social embodied intelligence over time. An egocentric episode illustrates four linked capabilities: grounding social cues (Attention), inferring the partners goal (Intention), deciding Egos response (Reaction), and evaluating the exchange (Interaction). Each query uses only observations up to the query time, without access to future evidence. intelligence as multi-stage decision process spanning Attention, Intention, Reaction, and Interaction, as shown in Figure 1. Specifically, Attention evaluates whether the model can localize the interaction partner from the first-person stream [19, 20] and integrate explicit multimodal cues, including gaze, gestures, body posture, emotional states, and speech, into an observable focus. Building on this evidence, Intention infers the partners underlying goal and identifies the earliest moment this goal becomes decidable. Reaction then shifts to the ego-agent, assessing its ability to select well-timed navigation, manipulation, communication, or justified inaction in response to the inferred intent to advance the exchange. Finally, Interaction tracks the evolving episode to evaluate the overall outcome against task completion, mutual understanding, and social norms. By aligning these capabilities within the same episodes, AIRIS assesses social cues, intent inference, response selection, and interaction outcomes under shared temporal framework. This enables stage-specific diagnosis of model strengths and weaknesses. To operationalize this evaluation, AIRIS aligns every social episode along four precise temporal anchors: T0 (social cue onset), T1 (when intent becomes inferable), T2 (ego-agent response onset), and T3 (interaction resolution). By querying models at specific moments τ using only the causal observation prefix up to that point, we prevent future evidence from leaking into online decisions. To capture the complexity and diversity of real-world social environments, AIRIS encompasses 8,000 questions across 357 egocentric video clips, spanning 11 diverse interaction contexts ranging from retail and market commerce to everyday social encounters and collaborative professional services. These questions probe 36 fine-grained capability dimensions systematically structured across the four A-I-R-I interaction stages. Our evaluation reveals that current social embodied competence is both fragmented across model families and miscalibrated over time. Leading general-purpose VLMs excel at perceptual cue grounding (up to 93.6% on Attention) and intent recognition, whereas embodied specialists lead on isolated response sub-decisions (up to 68.8% on Reaction). Yet no model closes the full online decision loop. Prior to intent decidability (τ < T1), model families prematurely guess specific intent on 26%-51% of queries instead of waiting for sufficient evidence. Furthermore, requiring simultaneous correctness across intervention timing, action domain, and concrete execution causes full-reaction accuracy to collapse below 14.7% across all 45 models. Current VLMs thus remain capable observers and post-hoc judges, rather than temporally calibrated social agents. Our contributions are threefold: Formalizing the Social Interaction Loop. We break down multi-party social interaction into an interdependent four-stage decision process (A-I-R-I), introducing time-anchored framework that bridges passive multimodal perception with proactive embodied action and social norm compliance. Ego-Centric Causal Streaming Benchmark. We present AIRIS, benchmark of 8,000 QA pairs across 11 diverse social contexts and 36 capability dimensions, evaluated under strict causal streaming protocol that mirrors ego-centric sensory constraints and eliminates future-information leakage. Exposing the Perception-Decision Gap. Across 45 models spanning general-purpose, embodied, streaming-video, and omni-modal families, AIRIS reveals that relatively strong social-cue perception and post-hoc assessment do not translate into evidence-calibrated anticipation or complete embodied reactions. Temporal calibration and end-to-end decision composition emerge as two major unresolved bottlenecks to reliable social embodied intelligence.

sections.title: 2.1 Benchmark Formulation
sections.content: Problem Formulation. We evaluate social embodied intelligence as an online decision process over firstperson stream, spanning Attention, Intention, Reaction, and Interaction. social episode is time-bounded interpersonal exchange observed as = {ot}Tmax , where each ot = (vt, at) contains only first-person RGB t=0 frames vt and acoustic signals at (raw audio for omni-modal models, or time-aligned ASR transcripts for 3 Figure 2 AIRIS construction pipeline. Web videos are screened, human-verified, and segmented into episodes. Clips then receive fully manual Attention labels and model-assisted, multi-annotator Intention, Reaction, and Interaction labels with group adjudication. Verified A-I-R-I annotations are templated into candidate question pool and expert-curated into the final benchmark. standard VLMs). At query time τ , model may access only the causal prefix Oτ = {ot τ }. Each question is evaluated from its designated observation prefix. The four task groups share episode annotations and temporal anchors, while their predictions are scored separately. Temporal Anchors. To track the progression of social exchange, we map the causal chain of each episode to four precise temporal anchors: T0 (Cue Onset): the first manifestation of social cue (e.g., gaze shift or gesture onset), marking the start of the Attention window. T1 (Decidability Onset): the earliest moment at which human experts can unambiguously determine the partners intent. T2 (Reaction Onset): the onset of the ego-agents substantive physical or verbal response. T3 (Interaction Resolution): the conclusion of the immediate exchange. The A-I-R-I Task Suite. To operationalize this causal timeline into measurable capabilities, AIRIS structures the evaluation into four interdependent task layers, encompassing 36 fine-grained capability dimensions, as shown in Figure 1. Full capability definitions appear in Supplementary Section C.1, with example questions and reviewed answers in Supplementary Sections E.1-E.4. All tasks are formulated as closed-set multiplechoice to ensure objective and reproducible evaluation. Specifically, the suite unfolds along the interaction timeline as follows: Attention (Understanding observable social cues): This layer models attention as sequential, two-step grounding process. First, the model must allocate the ego-agents focus to localize the potential interaction partner within complex environment. Second, it must analyze the partners own attention and observable state, including gaze and pointing targets, as well as gestures, poses, and emotions. By evaluating interactant identification and target anchoring strictly from the Oτ stream, this layer ensures the model correctly isolates the relevant person and their focus before inferring deeper intent. Intention (Inferring the partners latent goals): Given the grounded evidence, this layer asks what the partner is attempting to achieve. Intention is therefore timed inference of latent goal. First, the model must decide whether the goal is already supportable from Oτ . Second, only when τ T1 must it recover 4 that goal and select the visual, vocal, or verbal evidence that justifies the inference. For prefixes with τ < T1, Insufficient evidence is the explicitly correct answer. This strictly separates calibrated waiting from premature guessing. Reaction (Deciding ego-agent decisions): This layer shifts from interpreting the partner to deciding what the ego-agent should do now, given the inferred intent and the evidence available in Oτ . First, the model must make an engagement decision: whether to act, communicate, keep observing, or refrain. Second, only if engagement is warranted must it specify the action domain, and the concrete sub-action. Waiting and non-intervention remain valid targets when τ < T1 or when an action would interrupt an ongoing activity. Interaction (Evaluate completeness and norms): Evaluated post-hoc at τ T3, this layer assesses the episodes overall state and outcome. First, the model must track the episode state and detect whether social violation occurs, and if so of what type. Second, at τ T3 it must judge the completed exchange along task completeness, mutual understanding, spatial etiquette, physical demeanor, communication etiquette, and overall interaction category.

sections.title: 2.2 Dataset Construction
sections.content: To construct AIRIS under rigorous quality control, we employ six-layered human-model collaborative pipeline spanning video curation, structured annotation, and benchmark assembly (Figure 2). Quality assurance is incorporated throughout the pipeline: candidate videos undergo VLM screening and human verification, temporal proposals are manually refined, structured labels are reviewed and adjudicated, and every generated question receives expert inspection. This layered design prevents unverified model outputs from propagating directly into the benchmark and preserves traceable connection from each released question to its source clip, temporal context, and reviewed annotation. More details in Supplementary Sections C.3 and C.4. Keyword-guided video retrieval. We first define keyword inventory covering the target interaction contexts and use it to retrieve candidate egocentric videos from publicly accessible web platforms. At this stage, retrieval serves only to construct broad candidate pool; the presence of first-person viewpoint or an interpersonal exchange does not by itself qualify video for inclusion. Model-assisted eligibility screening. proprietary VLM screens candidate videos against five criteria: egocentric viewpoint, temporal continuity, audiovisual quality, content suitability, and interaction validity. These criteria distinguish usable first-person social exchanges from footage with disrupted event sequences, insufficient perceptual evidence, or no meaningful interpersonal interaction. Human reviewers reassess the model-approved subset using the same criteria; only videos passing both stages proceed to episode segmentation. Human-refined episode segmentation. For eligible videos, proprietary VLM analyzes the scene and proposes temporal boundaries for interaction episodes. Human reviewers verify the proposed episodes and refine their boundaries under the same annotation guidelines, preserving the context needed to interpret the exchange. The approved intervals are extracted as egocentric interaction clips. Layer-specific A-I-R-I annotation. We tailor the annotation protocol for each clip to the distinct evidential demands of the A-I-R-I layers. The Attention layer focuses on perceptually subtle yet directly observable social cues. To minimize missed cues and spatial-grounding errors from automated pre-annotation, we annotate this layer entirely by hand. One annotator identifies the interactant, observable social cues, their targets, and the corresponding spatial grounding, while second human reviewer verifies the resulting labels. For streaming Intention and Reaction annotations, whose temporal boundaries and semantic interpretations can be ambiguous, strong proprietary VLM and two human annotators separately propose candidate temporal anchors, partner intentions, and Ego responses based on the admissible causal prefixes. Interaction annotations follow the same model-assisted, multi-annotator protocol, covering both the evolving interaction state and resolved outcomes such as completeness, mutual understanding, and norm compliance. An expert panel reviews the candidate annotations, resolves disagreements against the video evidence, and determines the Figure 3 AIRIS composition. The inner ring shows the balanced A-I-R-I hierarchy; the outer ring illustrates the distribution across 11 interaction contexts. final labels. Model outputs therefore serve only as annotation proposals and are never accepted as ground truth without human verification. Template-based question compilation. The verified annotations are converted into candidate question pool using predefined templates associated with the 36 capability dimensions. Each generated item retains traceable link to its source clip, supporting annotation, admissible temporal context, and answer key. Streaming items expose only the causal observation prefix Oτ . In particular, Intention questions queried before T1 assign Insufficient evidence as the correct response rather than requiring premature intent prediction. Interaction-state and online-compliance questions likewise use the prefix available at their query time, whereas resolved outcome questions use the episode through T3. This construction prevents future evidence from entering online decisions while preserving complete episodes for retrospective outcome assessment. Expert question review and benchmark finalization. Finally, expert reviewers inspect each candidate item together with its video evidence, temporal scope, question, answer options, and proposed answer key. Reviewers retain valid items, revise correctable items, and remove questions with insufficient evidence, ambiguous or redundant options, non-unique answers, inconsistent temporal context, or future-information leakage. This question-level review is conducted separately from annotation adjudication because verified structured label does not necessarily yield an unambiguous evaluation item. The resulting review decisions control benchmark size while ensuring that every released question is supported by its designated visual, acoustic, and temporal evidence.

sections.title: 2.3 Evaluation Protocol and Metrics
sections.content: We evaluate AIRIS with balanced top-level score complemented by stage-specific diagnostic probes that penalize ungrounded, collapsed, or premature predictions. Individual items are scored in [0, 1] by exact match (single-choice, yes/no, and bounding-box selection) or set F1 (multi-choice), with invalid or unparseable outputs receiving zero credit. Aggregating item scores within each A-I-R-I stage yields four question-micro layer scores, namely SAtt, SInt, SRea, and SInter, whose unweighted mean defines the headline metric: Overall = 1 4 (SAtt + SInt + SRea + SInter) . (1) Beyond aggregate stage scores, we isolate the primary reasoning bottlenecks within each layer. For Attention, we report Semantic target (identifying the attended entity) and Grounding (localizing its bounding box) separately, as naming referent without spatial localization fails to support downstream embodied decisions. 6 For Intention, because insufficient evidence is the ground-truth label prior to T1, plain accuracy cannot distinguish calibrated waiting from lucky guessing. We therefore introduce the Intent Anticipation Score (IAS) to evaluate streamed intent recovery. For each event, let tf be the first query timestamp satisfying tf T1, and let T1 be the earliest timestamp from which the model maintains stable correctness. Discounting this margin by premature guessing yields the event-level score: IASevent = (1 FCR), where the False Commitment Rate (FCR) is the fraction of pre-T1 queries that prematurely commit to specific intent rather than abstaining. Macro-averaging IASevent across evaluable events gives the final IAS. For Reaction, we report Engage as the macro-F1 between active intervention and non-intervention classes to penalize collapsed policies, alongside strict Joint-EM diagnostic requiring simultaneous exact matches across engagement, action domain, subaction, and applicable speech function. Finally, Interaction evaluates Compliance across spatial, physical, and communication etiquette at episode resolution, as well as Violation, which treats violation present as the positive class to prevent exploitation of the heavily skewed negative baseline. sections.title: 2.4 Benchmark Statistics
sections.content: The AIRIS benchmark comprises 8,000 questions grounded in 357 egocentric clips and 276 source videos, totaling 10.91 hours of footage. Clip durations range from 3.0 to 767.3 seconds with mean of 110.0 seconds, capturing both brief encounters and extended interactions. The dataset averages 22.4 questions per clip and 11.46 sampled frames per question, comprehensively covering 36 capabilities, 11 contexts, and 230 fine-grained subscenes. These clips span diverse real-world settings as shown in Figure 3. The predominant categories are Market Commerce with 1,324 questions, Store Retail with 1,055, Work & Professional Services with 1,052, and Social Encounters with 976, alongside environments like dining, recreation, and wayfinding. Through rigorous expert curation, AIRIS maintains perfectly balanced top-level hierarchy that allocates exactly 2,000 questions to each A-I-R-I layer. To probe different reasoning facets, the benchmark employs four response formats: single-choice at 63.1%, multi-choice at 25.6%, bounding-box selection at 6.4%, and yes/no at 5.0%. Furthermore, 87.7% of questions feature streaming triggers and 41.1% incorporate speech context. To account for heterogeneous question density across clips, we report both per-capability and clip-macro metrics.

sections.title: 3.2 Experimental Results and Insights
sections.content: Table 2 presents the evaluation results of 37 representative models on the AIRIS benchmark. Closed-source models, led by Gemini-3.7-Flash, establish dominant baseline in perceptual grounding and intent recognition. Gemini-3.7-Flash achieves the highest overall score of 0.726 and significantly outperforms open-source counterparts in Attention at 0.936 and Intention at 0.569. Conversely, open-source models, particularly those fine-tuned for embodied tasks, demonstrate highly competitive or superior decision-making capabilities. HYEmbodied-VLM-1.0 achieves the highest overall Reaction score of 0.688, while Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct leads in Interaction compliance at 0.923 and violation detection at 0.589. More experimental results are provided in Supplementary Section D. The Perception-Decision Gap. We observe pronounced capability divide across the A-I-R-I causal chain (Figure 4a). While general-purpose VLMs excel at passive observation and semantic reasoning (Attention and Intention), their advantage vanishes in the downstream Reaction and Interaction layers. Instead, embodied-specific models take the lead in generating socially appropriate, executable responses. This divergence reveals that understanding does not naturally translate to doing; generating compliant embodied actions in dynamic social scenarios requires specialized action-oriented alignment beyond standard semantic pre-training. 8 Figure 4 Uneven performance across A-I-R-I capabilities. (a) A-I-R-I performance: category averages (thick, translucent) and best models (thin, markers). (b) Correct-intent rate vs. normalized interaction time. (c) Mean False Commitment Rate (FCR) before T1. Miscalibrated Causal Anticipation. Streaming intent anticipation remains critical bottleneck across all models. Even the leading Gemini-3.7-Flash reaches an Intent Anticipation Score (IAS) of only 0.237, and most models score near 0.1. The anticipation curves in Figure 4b make the temporal structure explicit. The correct intent rate stays low before the decidability onset (u < 0), climbs only after T1, and remains modest even at the reaction onset T2 (at most 0.5 for closed source models). Crucially, this early deficit is not calibrated waiting. As Figure 4c shows, the False Commitment Rate (FCR) before T1 remains substantial across categories (0.26 to 0.51). This fraction measures queries that commit to specific intent when insufficient evidence is the correct answer. Individual models range from near abstention (Phi-4-Multimodal, 0.08) to aggressive guessing (GLM-5.3-Flash, 0.64; Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, 0.63; GPT-5.6-Sol, 0.57). Even Gemini3.7-Flash commits in 42% of early queries. Current models thus fail anticipation in two opposite ways: overconfident premature commitment or blind passivity, rather than exercising the evidence gated inference the task rewards. No model closes the full reaction decision chain. Our reaction evaluation reports two complementary views: an aggregate score (R-All) crediting each sub-decision (engagement, action domain, and the concrete subaction or utterance) and stricter Joint-EM requiring all of them to be correct simultaneously for the same event. Each sub-decision is individually non-trivial, yet requiring them to hold jointly makes performance collapse multiplicatively. No model exceeds Joint-EM of 0.147, which is far below what the component scores alone would predict. Deciding whether to engage, or planning plausible subaction, is therefore not enough on its own; only their correct, end-to-end composition yields trustworthy social response. The strict lens accordingly re-orders the leaderboard. HY-Embodied-VLM-1.0, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and MiMoEmbodied-7B lead on aggregate Reaction (0.688, 0.655, 0.643) but fall to 0.028, 0.064, and 0.056 under the joint constraint. This integrative competence, rather than isolated perception, intent, or action, is the true prerequisite for trustworthy social embodied intelligence, and it remains largely unmet. Unrealized Architectural Dividends in Social Reasoning. Models specifically designed for native streaming video (e.g., JoyAI-VL, StreamingVLM) or omni-modal audio-visual processing (e.g., Qwen3-Omni) do not exhibit significant advantages over traditional frame-sampled VLMs (e.g., Qwen3.6-35B) in overall social embodied intelligence. The architectural benefits of continuous stream processing appear confined to low-level perception or speech dialogue. For tasks requiring deep Theory of Mind and adherence to complex social norms, these architectural shifts have not yet compensated for the lack of high-level social reasoning capabilities. Explicit reasoning does not reliably help streaming interaction. Allocating more test-time computation to explicit chain-of-thought is natural way to attack our causal streaming tasks, yet under identical streaming input, scored with thinking-aware re-parse that corrects systematic answer-parsing artifact, it brings no overall benefit: Qwen3.6-27B ties its no-think baseline (0.1 points) and Qwen3.6-35B drops (6.4 points), while Qwen3-Omni gains only marginally (2.9 points). 9 The effect is structured along the A-I-R-I reasoning tends to help chain (Figure 5a): multi-step spatial or decision sub-tasks, such as spatial grounding (A-Ground, +21.8 points for Qwen3.6-27B), but consistently hurts the columns that reward restraint under partial evidence, namely online intent (I-Online) and interaction compliance, across all models. The penalty is legible at the trace level (Figure 5b): accuracy falls with trace length, and although harder items independently elicit longer reasoning (a selection effect), thinking still widens the gap on the hardest Qwen3.6 items, whereas the restrained Qwen3-Omni is nearly unchanged. Traces carrying cognitiverevision markers (however, reconsider), present in about 77% of Qwen3.6 traces, lose roughly 27 to 30 points of accuracy: when perception is insufficient, extended deliberation fills the visual gap with language and overturns correct first instinct. Chain-of-thought optimized for static text problems is thus not yet adapted to the realtime, causally restrained demands of streaming social interaction. wait, Figure 5 Think versus no-think. sections.title: 4 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced AIRIS, first-person causal streaming benchmark evaluating social embodied intelligence as time-anchored progression across Attention, Intention, Reaction, and Interaction. Across 45 models, strong cue perception and intent recognition do not reliably translate to calibrated anticipation or complete embodied reactions. AIRIS thus shifts the evaluation focus from static social recognition to the dynamic timing of evidence sufficiency, action necessity, and response composition. These findings highlight key priorities for future models. First, models must preserve calibrated uncertainty before an intent becomes decidable, committing only when supported by observable evidence. Second, perception, inference, and action specification must be optimized as coupled decision process to ensure isolated strengths produce coherent reactions. Finally, test-time computation alone is insufficient; streaming reasoning must remain grounded in current sensory evidence and adapt its depth to uncertainty, avoiding the replacement of missing observations with unsupported verbal inference. By making timing, restraint, and decision composition measurable under causal observation, AIRIS establishes rigorous foundation for evaluating social embodied intelligence. Future work will extend this framework to interactive robot-in-the-loop settings, broader social contexts, and open-ended generation. Ultimately, this progress fosters human-centered embodied agents: ones that not only understand what people are doing, but also know when to wait, whether to act, and how to respond in ways that align with human social norms and facilitate seamless human-robot coordination.

sections.title: B Related Work
sections.content: B.1 Streaming and Proactive Video Understanding Most video-language benchmarks [6466] assume that model can inspect complete, temporally bounded clip before answering, whereas deployed assistants receive observations sequentially. On the model side, VideoLLM-online [67] introduced temporally aligned dialogue over continuous video streams and an asynchronous inference pipeline for real-time processing. Subsequent systems target complementary bottlenecks: Flash-VStream [58] compresses long-running visual context into context and augmentation memories for low-latency query answering, whereas Dispider [68] separates perception, decision, and reaction into asynchronous modules so that response generation does not suspend stream processing. More recently, Streamo [69] learns explicit silence, standby, and response states within single autoregressive sequence, coupling response timing with content generation across multiple streaming tasks. On the evaluation side, StreamingBench [7] distributes timestamped questions throughout stream, while OVO-Bench [8] organizes online understanding into backward tracing, real-time perception, and forward active responding, including waiting until sufficient evidence becomes available. OmniMMI and SocialOmni [70, 71] broaden this setting to multimodal interaction, proactive alerting, and turn taking. EgoSAT and StreamGaze [9, 72] evaluate temporal reasoning from strict egocentric prefixes, with the latter incorporating gaze. Complementary robotegocentric tracking research evaluates persistent target-person grounding over long horizons, from large-scale benchmarking to referring-then-tracking models [19, 20]. Recent work has also shifted from answering predefined queries to deciding when and how an assistant should respond. ViSpeak [73] extracts visual instructions from gestures and body language in streaming video; ESTPBench [22] evaluates proactive coherence and just-in-time responses; and ProAssist and EDITH [10, 74] use egocentric streams for proactive guidance and robot assistance. IPIBench [24] further evaluates proactive monitoring, task modification and cancellation, and interleaved reactive-proactive requests. EgoServe [75] frames proactive assistance as context-dependent intervention problem over multiple memory horizons. Existing streaming and proactive benchmarks predominantly focus on object-centric task execution or userdirected assistance, treating humans primarily as task performers or commanders. Building on their realtime protocols, AIRIS shifts the paradigm to social embodiment. It evaluates the ego-agent as social participant, diagnosing its ability to navigate interpersonal dynamics, anticipate social intents, and deliver norm-appropriate responses in shared environments. B.2 Multimodal Social Interaction Understanding foundational requirement for social embodied intelligence is the ability to perceive and interpret human behavior from heterogeneous social signals. Social-IQ [11] frames this ability as multimodal question answering over natural social situations, while Human-MME [26] and HumanPCR [27] provide broader evaluations spanning fine-grained human perception, comprehension, and reasoning. SIV-Bench [12] further structures social video understanding into social scene understanding, state reasoning, and dynamics prediction. Moving beyond answer accuracy, Social Genome [76] evaluates whether social inferences are explicitly grounded in visual, verbal, and vocal evidence as well as relevant external knowledge. complementary line grounds interaction evidence to relevant regions and participants [77, 78]. Recently, attention-prediction research further links gaze to human-object interactions and behavior-aware context, while explainable formulations connect where attention falls to what is attended and why [79, 80]. Robot-centric work models individual attributes, group context, intent, and social actions from onboard observations [81, 82]. SocialGesture [83] targets the recognition, temporal localization, and question answering of natural gestures in multi-person interactions. The MultiMediate challenge series [84, 85] evaluates conversational behaviors such as eye contact, backchannels, agreement, engagement, and bodily behavior in group discussions. The MMSI lineage [13, 86, 87] instead emphasizes identity-attributed social cues, including speaking targets and pronoun references, while GRASP [29] connects high-level social reasoning to participant-specific gaze and gesture evidence. At higher reasoning level, MuMA-ToM [14] evaluates goals, beliefs, and nested beliefs in embodied multi-agent interactions. In egocentric settings, EgoGazeVQA [88] studies gaze as an indicator of user intent, whereas R3VQA [28] represents belief, intent, desire, and emotion through mental-physical causal chains. Collectively, these benchmarks substantially advance the perception and interpretation of other peoples attention, references, intentions, and social states. AIRIS evaluates these capabilities alongside response selection, justified inaction, and assessment of observed interaction outcomes within the same time-anchored episodes. B.3 Social Norms and Embodied Decision Making Understanding others is insufficient for social embodiment: an agent must also determine what it should do, when it should act, and which otherwise feasible actions are socially inappropriate. EgoNormia [15] grounds this problem in egocentric video by evaluating socially appropriate next actions, their justifications, and acceptable alternatives under potentially competing physical-social norms. RobotEQ [16] similarly evaluates action permissibility and spatial grounding from robot-view scenes, with an emphasis on deciding how, when, and whether to act without explicit instructions. NormAct [17] extends norm evaluation to embodied planning, testing whether models can infer hidden social constraints and incorporate them into action sequences while still achieving an explicit task goal. The SHREC benchmark [89] evaluates whether foundation models can identify robots social errors and competencies, reason about their effects on interaction progression, and propose corrections. Should Help? [2] challenges the assumption that assistance is always desirable and formalizes whether help is appropriate in terms of human and robot skills together with the social benefits and costs to the recipient. NIABench [18] further formulates non-intrusive assistance as joint decision over when to act and what action to take while preserving the humans ongoing task flow. Embodied robotics has also operationalized particular dimensions of socially appropriate behavior. Habitat 3.0 [1] introduces human-in-the-loop social navigation and collaborative rearrangement tasks in which robots must coordinate with people, maintain distance, and yield shared space. VLM-Social-Nav and Social-LLaVA [90, 91] use vision-language models for socially aware navigation. SONAR [92] instead provides an adaptive norm-aware control architecture for social robots, combining explicit agent reasoning with learned contextual norms in human-robot conversations. These studies address complementary aspects of norm recognition, embodied planning, assistance, navigation, and robot-behavior assessment, but generally evaluate them as separate decision problems. AIRIS links norm-aware responses and justified inaction to the social evidence and inferred intent that precede them, enabling process-level diagnosis of both Reaction and Interaction within single time-anchored streaming episode.

It is organized into four parts: the formal capability ontology (Section C.1), the supplementary evaluation protocol and metrics (Section C.2), the expert annotation interfaces (Section C.3), and the expert annotation and audit process (Section C.4). C.1 A-I-R-I capability ontology AIRIS operationalizes social embodied intelligence as 36 separately scored capabilities: 19 in Attention, three in Intention, four in Reaction, and ten in Interaction (Tables 3-6). The decomposition is intentionally diagnostic. Attention asks what can be directly grounded in the observed scene; Intention asks what latent goal is supported by that evidence; Reaction asks what Ego should do at the current moment; and Interaction judges how the exchange actually unfolded. Thus, Interaction does not repeat the partner-intent label. Its labels describe episode phase, completion, mutual understanding, and Egos norm compliance. These labels are adjudicated post hoc using the complete episode, although every model query is still restricted to the released causal prefix. This stage establishes whom Ego should attend to and what directly observable social cues that person exhibits. C.2 Supplementary Evaluation Protocol and Metrics Building upon the core evaluation protocol in Section 2.3 of the main paper, this section defines the complete set of metrics used to isolate fine-grained reasoning bottlenecks across the 36 capabilities of AIRIS. These metrics are reported in the detailed evaluation tables (Section D.2) to prevent surface-level accuracy from masking deeper failure modes. Scoring and aggregation. Base items are scored by exact match (single-choice, yes/no, bounding-box) or set F1 (multi-choice). Empty, unparseable, and out-of-vocabulary responses score 0. The headline metric is the unweighted mean of the four question-micro layer scores: Overall = 1 4 (SAtt + SInt + SRea + SInter). Attention Metrics: Semantic Target & Spatial Localization: Semantic target assesses which entity social cue (e.g., gaze, pointing) refers to. Spatial localization evaluates its grounding over candidate boxes. Joint Identity-Localization: strict metric requiring both the semantic class and the spatial bounding box to match the reference simultaneously. If either fails, the joint score is 0. This penalizes models that name referent without localizing it, yielding non-executable percept. Nonverbal States: Accuracy on classifying body pose, physical stance, hand gesture, and observable emotion. 23 Multimodal Attribution: Set F1 score for identifying which observable modalities (gaze, hand movement, body posture, speech) provide the primary evidence for the current attentional focus. Intention Metrics: Intent Anticipation Score (IAS): Evaluates streamed intent recovery. Before the earliest supportable moment T1, insufficient evidence is the correct label. Let FCR be the False Commitment Rate (the fraction of pre-T1 queries prematurely committing to specific intent). For models reaching stable correctness at timestamp T1, we define an anticipation margin = clip((T2 p)/(T2 tf ), 0, 1), where tf is the first query at or after T1 (with = 0 if stability is never reached). The event-level score is IASevent = (1 FCR), and IAS is its macro average. Key-Moment & Online Accuracy: Key-moment evaluates accuracy at fixed expert-annotated query timestamps. Online evaluates accuracy across sampled temporal prefixes. Evidence Grounding: Set F1 score for identifying which specific observable cues (visual, vocal, or verbal) justify the inferred intent. Reaction Metrics: Engage: Macro-F1 between active intervention and idle/waiting classes. Chosen over plain accuracy to penalize collapsed policies on heavily imbalanced classes. Action Domain & Subaction: Action domain and Subaction use multi-label F1 to evaluate the broad response modalities and concrete actions Ego should employ. Speak subtype uses accuracy for communicative functions. Joint-EM: strict diagnostic for responses requiring the engagement, action domain, subaction, and any annotated speech subtype to match the reference simultaneously. Domain-Specific Diagnostics: Breaks down the Subaction + Speak scores by the required action domain (Communication, Navigation, Manipulation, Refrain/Idle) to isolate modality-specific performance. Interaction Metrics: State & Task Outcome: State tracks the current phase of the exchange (e.g., active engagement, disengagement). Task outcome judges whether the underlying social exchange succeeded, failed, or was aborted, and whether mutual understanding was achieved. Compliance: Equally averages spatial etiquette, physical demeanor, communication etiquette, and overall compliance category (τ T3). Violation: Equally averages online violation-presence F1, online violation type, and segment-level violation types. Violation present is the positive class to prevent exploitation of the skewed negative baseline. C.3 Expert Annotation Interfaces As shown in Figure 6, we developed two specialized web interfaces to facilitate the AIRIS annotation and auditing workflow. The first interface (Figure 6a) is designed for structured A-I-R-I annotation: it integrates egocentric video playback, spatial bounding-box annotation, time-aligned dense captions, and structured forms for recording observable attention cues, temporal anchors (T0 to T3), partner intentions, ego-agent reactions, and interaction attributes. The second interface (Figure 6b) is dedicated to question review and auditing, pairing each candidate question and its admissible video prefix with multiple-choice options and review controls for item-level inspection, editing, approval, or removal. Using the two interfaces above, the expert workflow proceeds in two stages. During structured A-I-R-I annotation, annotators review the video stream, identify and refine critical temporal anchors (T0 to T3), manually ground observable attention cues, and adjudicate structured labels for the partners intention, the ego-agents reaction, and episode-level interaction compliance strictly based on observable evidence. During question auditing, experts inspect the generated question-answer pairs, distractors, and temporal constraints item by itemretaining valid items, revising correctable ones, and removing flawed candidatesto ensure that every released evaluation item is unambiguous, uniquely answerable from the causal prefix, and free from future-information leakage.

sections.content: E.1 Attention cases Figures 7-25 present representative streaming examples for all 19 Attention capabilities. To balance visual consistency with scenario diversity, adjacent capabilities are grouped within four expertly verified episodes: professional craft workshop, retail checkout, an outdoor farmers market, and card shop checkout. Each panel displays only the causal observation prefix available at the designated query time, followed by the original options and the verified gold response. For tasks requiring spatial or combined semantic and spatial reasoning, candidate bounding boxes are additionally overlaid on the final visible frame. E.2 Intention cases Figures 26-31 provide two representative examples for each of the three Intention capabilities: key-moment intention recognition, temporal intention recognition, and intention evidence grounding. The paired cases cover distinct social contexts and evidence conditions, including both supportable intentions and an early prefix for which the calibrated response is insufficient evidence. Each panel shows only the causal video prefix and the ASR available by the marked query time, together with the original answer choices and reviewed gold response. E.3 Reaction cases Figures 32-38 provide representative examples spanning the four Reaction capabilities: engagement decision, action-domain selection, subaction selection, and speech-function selection. The paired checkout and servicewindow scenes illustrate how AIRIS progresses from deciding whether Ego should respond to specifying the appropriate response modality, concrete action, and, when speech is warranted, communicative function. Each panel uses only the causal video prefix and any ASR available by the marked query time, and retains the original answer choices and reviewed gold response. E.4 Interaction cases Figures 39-48 provide one representative example for each of the ten Interaction capabilities. The query-time cases assess the evolving interaction state and whether social violation is present at the current prefix, whereas the segment-level cases assess completion, mutual understanding, spatial, physical, and communication compliance, overall compliance category, and the violation types observed over the episode. Together, the examples cover both compliant and violating interactions across retail-counter, reception, sales-floor, and simulated skills exam settings.
